new.title: Climb to the Sacré-Cœur
new.desc: The white basilica on top of the Butte Montmartre is the highest natural point in Paris, and the steps below it are the city's favourite free grandstand.
new.tip: Skip the funicular queue and take the stairs through Square Louise Michel; come early in the morning, before the crowds and the buskers arrive.
new.q: Basilique du Sacré-Cœur de Montmartre, Paris

new.title: Shake hands with Le Passe-Muraille
new.desc: A bronze man is stuck halfway through a wall on Place Marcel Aymé, a tribute to the Montmartre writer's story about a clerk who could walk through walls.
new.tip: His left hand is polished gold from all the handshakes. Carry on to nearby Place Dalida and the leafy Villa Léandre for the quiet side of the hill.
new.q: Le Passe-Muraille, Place Marcel Aymé, Paris

new.title: Find the vineyard of Montmartre
new.desc: The Clos Montmartre is a tiny working vineyard on the north slope of the hill, a last reminder of the days when the Butte was covered in vines.
new.tip: You can only peer in through the fence from Rue des Saules, but the Musée de Montmartre next door looks down on the vines from its gardens.
new.q: Vigne du Clos Montmartre, Rue des Saules, Paris

new.title: Walk up the grand staircase of the Opéra Garnier
new.desc: The Palais Garnier is Second Empire Paris at its most extravagant: marble, gold leaf, a sweeping staircase and a foyer built to be seen in.
new.tip: You can visit during the day without a performance ticket; the auditorium is sometimes closed for rehearsals, so check before you go.
new.q: Palais Garnier, Place de l'Opéra, Paris

new.title: Wander Passage Jouffroy and Passage Verdeau
new.desc: Two glass-roofed 19th-century arcades run one after the other off the Grands Boulevards, lined with toy shops, old bookshops, print dealers and walking-stick sellers.
new.tip: Start on Boulevard Montmartre next to the Musée Grévin and keep walking north; Passage Verdeau begins right across Rue de la Grange-Batelière.
new.q: Passage Jouffroy, Boulevard Montmartre, Paris

new.title: Have tea in the garden of the Musée de la Vie Romantique
new.desc: At the end of a cobbled lane in the Nouvelle Athènes quarter sits the painter Ary Scheffer's shuttered villa, where George Sand and Chopin were regulars. It reopened in 2026 after a long renovation.
new.tip: The tea room is in the greenhouse facing the rose garden; you can easily miss the entrance, a narrow alley off Rue Chaptal.
new.q: Musée de la Vie romantique, 16 rue Chaptal, Paris

new.title: Get lost in Père Lachaise
new.desc: The most visited cemetery in the world is a hilly maze of cobbled lanes, mossy tombs and famous names, from Oscar Wilde and Chopin to Edith Piaf and Jim Morrison.
new.tip: Enter from the top near Gambetta and walk downhill to the main gate on Boulevard de Ménilmontant; take a photo of the map at the entrance.
new.q: Cimetière du Père-Lachaise, Paris

new.title: Watch the sun set from Parc de Belleville
new.desc: The terrace at the top of this steep park has one of the widest views over Paris, with the sun going down behind the Eiffel Tower and hardly a tour group in sight.
new.tip: Go straight to the belvedere on Rue Piat at the top of the park, and bring a drink: this is where the neighbourhood comes for its evening apéro.
new.q: Belvédère de Belleville, Rue Piat, Paris

new.title: See the painted walls of Rue Dénoyez
new.desc: This short Belleville side street has been an open-air canvas since the 2000s, covered layer upon layer by graffiti writers and street artists.
new.tip: It is a two minute walk from Belleville metro; the walls change constantly, so come by daylight and you may catch someone at work.
new.q: Rue Dénoyez, Paris

new.title: Stroll through La Campagne à Paris
new.desc: On top of an old gypsum quarry near Porte de Bagnolet, about ninety little brick houses with front gardens form a village that was built as a workers' cooperative in the early 1900s.
new.tip: Take one of the stair streets up from Rue du Capitaine-Ferber and loop along Rue Irénée-Blanc and Rue Jules-Siegfried. People live here, so keep it quiet.
new.q: La Campagne à Paris, Rue Irénée-Blanc, Paris

new.title: Climb the Butte Bergeyre
new.desc: A handful of quiet streets sit on their own little hilltop next to the Buttes-Chaumont, with a shared garden, a pocket vineyard and a clear view across to the Sacré-Cœur.
new.tip: Walk up the staircase from Avenue Simon-Bolivar and head for the western edge on Rue Georges-Lardennois, where the vines and the view are.
new.q: Butte Bergeyre, Rue Georges-Lardennois, Paris

new.title: Explore the villas of La Mouzaïa
new.desc: Behind the Buttes-Chaumont, narrow cobbled lanes called villas are lined with small houses, lampposts and wisteria, built low because the ground below is an old quarry.
new.tip: Get off at Danube or Botzaris and zigzag between Rue de Mouzaïa and Rue du Général-Brunet; late spring is best, when everything is in bloom.
new.q: Rue de Mouzaïa, Paris

new.title: Watch the Pont de Crimée lift
new.desc: The last lift bridge in Paris has been raising its roadway for canal boats since 1885, and still goes up thousands of times a year.
new.tip: When a boat approaches, cross on the footbridge beside it to watch the whole deck rise between its four pulleys.
new.q: Pont levant de la rue de Crimée, Paris

new.title: Visit Lafayette's grave at Picpus
new.desc: Hidden behind a convent door, this private cemetery holds the mass graves of people guillotined on nearby Place de la Nation in 1794, and the tomb of the Marquis de Lafayette.
new.tip: It only opens for a few hours in the afternoon and not every day, so check before you set off; ring at 35 Rue de Picpus.
new.q: Cimetière de Picpus, 35 rue de Picpus, Paris

new.title: Eat at Bouillon Chartier
new.desc: A Belle Époque workers' canteen with brass luggage racks, huge mirrors and waiters in black waistcoats, still serving plain French classics at low prices more than a century on.
new.tip: They take no reservations at this address, so come outside peak hours; you will share a table and your bill is scribbled on the paper tablecloth.
new.q: Bouillon Chartier Grands Boulevards, 7 rue du Faubourg Montmartre, Paris

new.title: Queue for an escargot at Du Pain et des Idées
new.desc: A bakery in a listed 19th-century shop near the canal, loved for its crusty pain des amis and its escargots, spiral pastries filled with things like pistachio and chocolate.
new.tip: It is closed at weekends. Buy your pastry and eat it on the canal bank, two streets away.
new.q: Du Pain et des Idées, 34 rue Yves Toudic, Paris

new.title: Open a bottle at Le Verre Volé
new.desc: One of the places that started the natural wine wave in Paris: a tiny cave à manger where you pick a bottle off the shelf and drink it with very good bistro cooking.
new.tip: There are only a handful of tables, so book ahead; ask the staff what to drink rather than hunting for a wine list.
new.q: Le Verre Volé, 67 rue de Lancry, Paris

new.title: Go for a curry in Passage Brady
new.desc: This covered arcade from 1828 has turned into a corridor of Indian and Pakistani restaurants, grocers and barbers, with spice smells drifting under the old glass roof.
new.tip: Enter at 46 Rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis for the covered part; the grocers here are also the place to stock up on spices.
new.q: Passage Brady, 46 rue du Faubourg Saint-Denis, Paris

new.title: Drink from the barrel at Le Baron Rouge
new.desc: A tiny, noisy wine bar beside the Marché d'Aligre where barrels are stacked to the ceiling and regulars bring empty bottles to fill straight from the tap.
new.tip: Go on a Sunday towards the end of the market, when oysters are opened outside and everyone stands on the pavement with a glass of white.
new.q: Le Baron Rouge, 1 rue Théophile Roussel, Paris

new.title: Look up at Le Train Bleu
new.desc: The station restaurant on the first floor of the Gare de Lyon is a gilded Belle Époque hall, its ceilings painted with the sunny destinations the trains were heading for.
new.tip: A full meal is a splurge and needs a reservation, but you can also just have a coffee or a drink in the bar lounge and take in the room.
new.q: Le Train Bleu, Gare de Lyon, Paris

new.title: Have a proper bistro dinner at Bistrot Paul Bert
new.desc: Tiled floor, chalkboard menu, zinc bar: this is the textbook Paris bistro, famous for its steak au poivre with frites and a Paris-Brest big enough to share.
new.tip: Reserve by phone a few days ahead; the same street has a small cluster of sister addresses if it is full.
new.q: Bistrot Paul Bert, 18 rue Paul Bert, Paris

new.title: Pick a pastry at Boulangerie Utopie
new.desc: A prize-winning neighbourhood bakery near Oberkampf, known for playful flavours such as black sesame and charcoal next to very serious croissants and baguettes.
new.tip: The queue moves quickly. Weekends bring special creations that sell out before lunch.
new.q: Boulangerie Utopie, 20 rue Jean-Pierre Timbaud, Paris

new.title: Squeeze into Septime La Cave
new.desc: The wine shop of the celebrated restaurant Septime doubles as a pocket-sized bar, pouring very natural wines by the glass with a few small plates.
new.tip: No reservations and barely any seats: arrive when it opens for the apéro and expect to stand with your glass.
new.q: Septime La Cave, 3 rue Basfroi, Paris

new.title: Join the guinguette at Rosa Bonheur
new.desc: A Swiss-style chalet inside the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont turned into an easy-going open-air tavern, with tapas, rosé and dancing as the evening goes on.
new.tip: Arrive before the park closes for the night: after that you can stay, but newcomers queue at a single gate on the south side.
new.q: Rosa Bonheur, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, Paris

new.title: Start the day at Les Vins du Matin
new.desc: A neighbourhood café set up in a former wine store in the north of the 18th, far from the Montmartre crowds and picked by Le Fooding for its natural wines.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk through the Halle Pajol gardens a few streets away, a converted railway depot.
new.q: Les Vins du Matin, 73 rue Riquet, Paris

new.title: Walk the Coulée Verte above the rooftops
new.desc: Long before New York's High Line, Paris planted a garden on a disused railway viaduct. The path runs car-free from Bastille towards the Bois de Vincennes, level with the third-floor windows.
new.tip: Take the stairs up from Avenue Daumesnil just behind the Opéra Bastille; the arches below, the Viaduc des Arts, house craft workshops.
new.q: Coulée verte René-Dumont, Avenue Daumesnil, Paris

new.title: Cross the bridge to the Temple de la Sibylle
new.desc: The Buttes-Chaumont is a former quarry turned into a wild, hilly park with a lake, a grotto with a waterfall and a little temple perched on a cliff in the middle.
new.tip: Reach the island over the suspension footbridge designed by Gustave Eiffel, then look for the grotto on the south bank of the lake.
new.q: Temple de la Sibylle, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, Paris

new.title: Sit on the edge of the Canal Saint-Martin
new.desc: Iron footbridges, locks and plane trees line this 19th-century canal, and on warm evenings half of eastern Paris sits along the quay with its legs dangling over the water.
new.tip: Climb one of the arched footbridges to watch a boat go through the locks, then pick a spot on Quai de Valmy or Quai de Jemmapes.
new.q: Canal Saint-Martin, Quai de Valmy, Paris

new.title: Swim in the Bassin de la Villette
new.desc: In summer the widest stretch of the canal becomes part of Paris Plages, with free floating pools on the Quai de la Loire, pétanque courts and pedal boats and canoes at the boating base.
new.tip: The pools have a limited capacity, so go on a weekday morning; the rest of the year the quays are a favourite pétanque and picnic spot.
new.q: Bassin de la Villette, Quai de la Loire, Paris

new.title: Watch a film on the lawn at La Villette
new.desc: Every summer the Parc de la Villette puts up a giant screen for its open-air film festival, and thousands of Parisians spread out picnic blankets on the grass at dusk.
new.tip: Come well before sunset with a picnic to get a good patch of lawn, and bring a jumper for when it gets dark.
new.q: Prairie du Triangle, Parc de la Villette, Paris

new.title: Catch a gig at La Maroquinerie
new.desc: A former leather workshop in Ménilmontant with a sunken stage that fits a few hundred people; plenty of future stars played here before anyone knew their names.
new.tip: Come early for a drink in the courtyard upstairs; La Bellevilloise, another concert and party venue, is right next door on Rue Boyer.
new.q: La Maroquinerie, 23 rue Boyer, Paris

new.title: Discover outsider art at the Halle Saint-Pierre
new.desc: An iron market hall at the foot of the Sacré-Cœur gardens now shows art brut and outsider art: strange, obsessive work by self-taught artists you will not see in the big museums.
new.tip: Exhibitions change a few times a year, and the bookshop on the ground floor is worth a browse even if you skip the show.
new.q: Halle Saint-Pierre, 2 rue Ronsard, Paris

new.title: Hang out on the tracks at La REcyclerie
new.desc: The old Ornano station of the Petite Ceinture railway is now a café and canteen with an urban farm, a repair workshop and a long terrace along the disused tracks.
new.tip: It is right by Porte de Clignancourt metro. From here you can also walk a short opened stretch of the Petite Ceinture towards Rue des Poissonniers.
new.q: La REcyclerie, 83 boulevard Ornano, Paris

new.title: Ride a pedal carousel at the Musée des Arts Forains
new.desc: Bercy's old wine warehouses hide a collection of antique fairground rides that you are allowed to use, including an 1897 carousel of bicycles powered by its own riders.
new.tip: Visits are guided and by reservation only, except around Christmas, when the Festival du Merveilleux opens the halls for free wandering.
new.q: Musée des Arts Forains, 53 avenue des Terroirs de France, Paris

new.title: Row a boat on Lac Daumesnil
new.desc: On the Paris edge of the Bois de Vincennes, a lake with two islands is made for an hour in a rowing boat. Next to it stands a pagoda that houses the largest Buddha in Europe.
new.tip: Walk in from Porte Dorée metro; the boat hire is at the western tip of the lake. The pagoda only opens on festival days, but you can see it from the path.
new.q: Lac Daumesnil, Bois de Vincennes, Paris
